title: Graph Neural Networks
blurb: Tests message passing and the GCN's normalised aggregation, why structure alone can classify nodes, random-walk embeddings, TransE's h + r ≈ t, transductive against inductive models, and what the karate club and toy knowledge graph showed.

questions.prompt: What is the one idea behind every GNN variant, per the chapter?
options: The whole graph is flattened into one vector first.
Nodes are sorted by degree before processing.
Each node aggregates its neighbours, then transforms.
Each node is classified using only its own features.
questions.explanation: GCN, GraphSAGE and GAT all follow this pattern. Stacking layers widens how far information reaches.

refLinks.label: §79.2.1 Message Passing: The One Idea Behind Every GNN Variant

questions.prompt: How many hops away can a 2-layer GCN draw information from?
questions.explanation: Each layer aggregates one hop. A 2-layer GCN can't use a node 3 or more hops away, however important.

refLinks.label: §79.2.1 Message Passing: The One Idea Behind Every GNN Variant

questions.prompt: Two nodes share one edge. With self-loops, A + I = [[1, 1], [1, 1]] and each degree is 2. What is each entry of D^(−1/2)(A + I)D^(−1/2)?
questions.explanation: Each entry is 1 / (√2 × √2) = 0.5, so each node averages itself and its neighbour equally.

questions.prompt: Why does the GCN add self-loops with + I?
options: So each node includes itself
So high-degree nodes dominate the average
So the matrix becomes invertible
So the graph becomes directed
questions.explanation: Without self-loops, a node's update would use only its neighbours. The degree normalisation stops high-degree nodes dominating.

refLinks.label: §79.2.1 Message Passing: The One Idea Behind Every GNN Variant

questions.prompt: The GCN was given the identity matrix as features. What did that show?
options: The model needed no training to classify nodes.
Node features always hurt GCN accuracy.
Identity features are the best choice for real fraud data.
Connectivity alone was enough signal.
questions.explanation: Each node had only a one-hot ID, yet 29 of 30 unlabelled nodes were classified correctly. Real systems would add features too.

refLinks.label: §79.2.2 Why This Needs No Node Features At All

questions.prompt: What NLP idea does the random-walk embedding borrow?
options: Byte-pair encoding, merging frequent node pairs
Attention, treating each node as a token in a transformer
Skip-gram, treating each walk as a sentence of node IDs
TF-IDF, weighting nodes by how rare they are
questions.explanation: Nodes that co-occur in many walks end up with similar embeddings, just as co-occurring words do.

refLinks.label: §79.2.3 node2vec: Borrowing word2vec’s Trick, Applied to Walks Instead of Sentences

questions.prompt: The tutorial ran 20 walks from each of the karate club's 34 nodes. How many walks is that?
questions.explanation: 34 × 20 = 680 walks, producing 23,120 centre-context pairs for skip-gram.

questions.prompt: How were labels used for the random-walk embeddings?
options: Only to check the result, never to train it
To weight the skip-gram loss per faction
To pick which walks to keep during training
To initialise the embeddings before training
questions.explanation: Training was fully unsupervised. Labels only measured how often nearest neighbours shared a faction.

questions.prompt: What geometric bet does TransE make?
options: Each fact gets its own separate vector.
Entities of the same type share one vector.
For true facts, head + relation ≈ tail.
A relation is a rotation of the head vector.
questions.explanation: True triples should satisfy h + r ≈ t better than corrupted ones. Rotations are RotatE's idea.

questions.prompt: Why does TransE struggle when a company has several owners?
options: Ownership relations are always negative vectors.
One translation can't hit several tails.
TransE can't store more than one fact per entity.
Several owners make the graph undirected.
questions.explanation: h + r is a single point, so it can't be close to many distinct tails. TransR, RotatE and ComplEx address this.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 79.3 warn against judging TransE on Hits@1 alone?
options: Hits@1 rewards wrong answers.
A near miss counts as a total miss.
Hits@1 is always 1.0 on small graphs.
Hits@1 can't be computed for typed relations.
questions.explanation: Mean rank and Hits@3 show near misses. Here Hits@1 was 0.923, but Hits@3 was 1.000.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that a GCN is transductive?
options: It can't natively handle unseen nodes.
It uses attention to weight neighbours.
It needs no labels at all.
It can classify nodes from any graph without retraining.
questions.explanation: GraphSAGE learns an aggregation function that applies to unseen nodes. GAT adds attention.

questions.prompt: The GCN classified 29 of 30 unlabelled karate-club nodes correctly. What accuracy is that? Give four decimal places.
questions.explanation: 29 / 30 = 0.9667, from just 4 labelled nodes and no node attributes.

questions.prompt: TransE's mean rank over 13 test facts was 1.0769. If 12 facts ranked first, where did the last rank?
A team plans to label thousands of nodes for a GCN. What does the chapter suggest checking first?
options: Whether labels can be skipped by using random features
Whether TransE can replace the GCN for node labels
Whether a deeper GCN needs even more labels
Whether unsupervised embeddings already suffice
questions.explanation: Unsupervised walk embeddings recovered 94% faction agreement with zero labels. Labelling is a real cost worth testing before paying.

bookExercises.prompt: State the "message passing" idea shared by every GNN variant in one sentence, and explain what it means for a 2-layer GCN's "field of view."
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Each node updates its own representation by aggregating its neighbours' representations, then applying a learned transformation. A 2-layer GCN's "field of view" is limited to nodes within 2 hops: its output for any node has only ever been influenced by that node's direct neighbours and its neighbours' neighbours, nothing further.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three models covered (GCN, node2vec, TransE) and state which one(s) require no labels during training.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: GCN, node2vec, TransE. node2vec and TransE both require no labels during training: they are fully unsupervised, learning purely from graph structure (random walks for node2vec, the `h + r ≈ t` constraint for TransE).

bookExercises.prompt: Using the GCN Worked Example's measured result (96.67% test accuracy from only 4 of 34 labelled nodes, identity-matrix features), explain what this specifically proves about where the model's predictive signal came from, given that no node carried any real attribute information.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Since the input features were the identity matrix (every node given only a one-hot marker of its own identity, no real attribute information whatsoever), any predictive signal the model used to correctly classify 29 of 30 unlabelled test nodes could only have come from the graph's connectivity pattern itself, propagated outward from the 4 labelled nodes through repeated neighbourhood aggregation. This directly proves that graph structure alone, with zero node attributes, carries enough signal to recover the correct faction labels for the overwhelming majority of nodes.

bookExercises.prompt: Using node2vec's measured result (94.12% same-faction rate vs. 54.90% random baseline), explain why comparing against the random-embedding baseline, not just reporting 94.12% alone, is necessary to interpret this number correctly.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Reporting 94.12% alone doesn't establish whether that number is actually good. Without a comparison point, a reader has no way to know if 94.12% represents strong structural signal or is simply what any reasonable embedding (even a poor or random one) would achieve on this particular graph. The random-embedding baseline (54.90%), embeddings with no learned structure at all, just random vectors, establishes the floor: since node2vec's 94.12% is dramatically above that floor, the result demonstrates real, learned structural signal, not an artifact of how the evaluation itself is set up.

bookExercises.prompt: A team has a large graph with almost no labelled nodes and a fixed budget for manual labelling. Using this chapter's Worked Example (GCN vs. node2vec results) and Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say about how to prioritise their labelling effort.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "Given a limited labelling budget, this chapter's own measured results suggest starting with an unsupervised approach like node2vec, which recovered 94.12% same-faction agreement using zero labels at all. Spend the labelling budget checking that result against a small validation sample rather than assuming labels are needed to train anything at all. If node2vec's unsupervised structure already captures most of what's needed, the GCN's label-dependent approach (which needed labels for training, not just checking) may not be worth the labelling cost it requires."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 79.3 warns against evaluating TransE with only Hits@1. Using the Worked Example's measured Hits@1 (0.9231) vs. Hits@3 (1.0000), construct a concrete scenario (a specific query) where Hits@1 alone would understate the model's real usefulness for a human reviewing its top-3 suggestions.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Consider the query `'Acme Corp OWNED_BY ?'` from the Worked Example, where the top-3 predictions were `['Zenith Holdings', 'Orion Group', 'Acme Corp']` with the correct answer (Zenith Holdings) ranking first in this specific case, but imagine a different query where the correct answer ranked 2nd or 3rd instead of 1st. Hits@1 alone would score this as a complete failure (0), even though a human reviewer looking at the top-3 suggestions would immediately spot the correct answer sitting right there in the list. Hits@3 (which was a perfect 1.0000 across the whole evaluation set) captures that "close, and practically still useful" case that Hits@1 would discard entirely, which matters a great deal for any real system where a human reviews a shortlist rather than blindly trusting only the single top prediction.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about TransE's known limitation with 1-to-many relations (e.g. a company with multiple owners), referenced in this chapter's Trade-offs. Explain in your own words, using the `h + r ≈ t` geometric constraint, exactly why one shared relation vector `r` cannot correctly place `h + r` close to two genuinely different tail entities simultaneously.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The `h + r ≈ t` constraint forces a single shared vector `r` (e.g. for `OWNED_BY`) to, when added to a given head entity's vector `h`, land close to exactly one point in embedding space. If a company `h` genuinely has two different owners `t1` and `t2`, satisfying the constraint would require `h + r` to be simultaneously close to both `t1` and `t2`. But `h + r` is one fixed point, and it can only be close to both `t1` and `t2` if those two tail entities are themselves already close together in embedding space (which they generally have no independent reason to be, since they're different, unrelated entities). This is a genuine geometric contradiction for a true 1-to-many relation, not merely a training difficulty. No amount of additional training resolves it, which is exactly why TransE structurally cannot represent this class of relation well, motivating successor models like RotatE that use richer geometric operations than simple vector addition.
